newsitem.title: USA: Rail rivals defend Conrail proposals to shippers.
newsitem.headline: Rail rivals defend Conrail proposals to shippers.

text.p: A day before a meeting of top executives involved in the battle for Conrail, each side claimed on Thursday its proposal would offer better service to freight shippers.

Speaking to a gathering of coal shippers at the National Mining Association's annual transportation seminar here, executives from CSX Corp and Conrail sought to reassure shippers that a merger of the two companies would not result in sharply higher freight rates, while Norfolk Southern Corp maintained that its plan offered shippers a more balanced rail network.
"Conrail and CSX offer the greatest amount of synergy potential," said Conrail senior vice president Timothy Dwyer. "Our merger proposal is not about foreclosing inter-line competition."

The chairmen of Conrail and CSX have agreed on a cash and stock merger worth $9.5 billion, while rival bidder Norfolk Southern has offered $115 a share for Conrail, or $10.3 billion. With the takeover battle at a virtual stalemate, the companies scheduled a meeting for tomorrow to resolve the impasse.
But for now, both sides continued to defend their original proposals.

"We are committed to dealing with two-to-one customer locations," Dwyer said, citing as examples the merger of Union Pacific Corp with Southern Pacific in 1996, and Burlington Northern with Sante Fe railroad in 1995.
Two-to-one locations occur when a shipper who previously was able to choose between two railroad companies at a specific location must contend with a single carrier following a merger.

In the case of BNSF and UP-SP, the number one and two railroads in the U.S., the companies agreed to grant trackage rights to their competitors to appease shippers and regulators worried at the possibility of a monopoly.

Dwyer said the advantages of a CSX-Conrail deal would become fully apparent in March, when the companies are slated to file their merger proposal to the Surface Transportation Board, the regulatory authority that oversees the railroads.
Ray Sharp, vice president for coal and sales marketing at CSX Transportation, said the deal would be a "good news" story for both coal shippers and utilities.
"This merger creates a more unified rail system...so that shippers will no longer have to depend on two or three railroads to get their freight moved."
Meanwhile, Norfolk Southern separately reiterated its claim on Conrail, saying its offer was "superior in every way."
"A Norfolk Southern-Conrail combination would more evenly balance competition in almost any measure imaginable, but particularly on the coal side," he said.

Fox told the audience packed with coal shippers that a link-up of Norfolk Southern and Conrail would fairly evenly divide rail carriers' access to power plants in the eastern half of the country. By contrast, a CSX-Conrail merger would give the newly formed company exclusive access to three-fourths of the region's utilities, he said.
Coal shipments between mines and utilities account for about 40 percent of all major rail freight transportation in the U.S., and about 20 percent of their annual revenue.
But shippers say they remained wary of any consolidation.
"We highly endorse competition," said Joseph Lema, vice president of the National Mining Association. "There is less of a threat of difficulties if the status quo remained."

Lema told Reuters that while either of the two merger proposals would offer substantially improved service to some coal shippers, many others would be left captive to a single railroad. The trade association has not taken an official position in the Conrail fight.
